analysis.one_liner: Protects people who cross state lines for abortions from state penalties and interference.
analysis.headline: The bill had 187 House supporters, all Democrats, but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court ended the federal right to abortion, some states penalize residents who travel out of state for the procedure. This bill would bar anyone enforcing state law from preventing, restricting, or retaliating against a patient who travels to another state for a legal abortion, anyone who helps them travel, providers who serve out-of-state patients, and the interstate shipping of FDA-approved abortion pills. Patients and providers could sue in federal court for damages, and the Justice Department could sue to stop violators.
analysis.who_benefits: People in states with abortion bans who need to cross state lines for care, the friends and family members who help them get there, and the clinics, doctors, nurses, and pharmacists who serve out-of-state patients. The bill does not require any state to allow abortion; it protects the right to obtain a lawful abortion elsewhere.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients crossing state lines for abortion care

how_it_helps.text: No person enforcing state law may prevent, restrict, or retaliate against a patient's ability to travel across a state line for a legal abortion, or against anyone helping them travel [S3].

Providers who give legal abortions to out-of-state residents, and anyone who assists them, are protected from state-law interference, covering physicians, nurses, midwives, physician assistants, and pharmacists [S3].
The interstate movement of FDA-approved abortion drugs is protected from state interference [S3].

A person harmed by a violation can sue in federal court for injunctions, compensatory damages including economic losses and emotional distress, and attorney's fees; the Attorney General may also sue [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State governments that enforce abortion bans would lose their ability to punish residents for traveling out of state, to penalize in-state helpers of out-of-state travel, and to block the shipping of abortion pills through their borders. Anyone whose state-law enforcement actions are challenged could face federal lawsuits and damages.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not require any state to permit abortion, and it protects only services that are lawful in the state where they are provided, so it offers no help to patients who cannot afford to travel or find care [S3].

It strips state officials of authority they currently exercise: anyone implementing state abortion law could be sued in federal court for stopping a patient's out-of-state travel or the shipment of abortion pills, a limit on state authority opponents would call an overreach of federal power [S3].

Enforcement relies on lawsuits after the fact; a patient who has already been prosecuted or detained by a state could recover damages, but the bill does not directly block state criminal prosecutions [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients in states with bans, the protections are real but partial: they guard travel, helpers, providers, and pill shipments, yet cannot create care where none exists locally or cover the cost of travel. The cost falls on state governments, which lose one enforcement tool against interstate abortion access. The main design weakness is that remedies come through civil suits after harm has occurred.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its Health Subcommittee, and stayed there; it never came up for a vote in committee or on the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lizzie Fletcher introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, and 186 House colleagues joined as cosponsors, all of them Democrats [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S1].
On February 10, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was taken for the rest of the 118th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State officials enforcing abortion bans keep their current authority to penalize interstate abortion travel and shipments, and the status quo remains unchanged.

for.name: Lizzie Fletcher
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 186 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republican joined.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Republican majority)
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or vote on the bill; it was referred to the Health Subcommittee on February 10, 2023, and stayed there.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor action during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 186 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sole sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill shields providers who serve out-of-state patients from state retaliation, and gives them a federal cause of action with damages and attorney's fees. Their interest in operating freely matches patients' interest in access.
Anyone implementing state abortion law could no longer penalize residents for out-of-state travel, penalize helpers, or block interstate shipment of abortion pills without facing federal lawsuits.
